title: Learning
summary: Learning is a relatively durable change in behaviour due to experience. Temporary changes, changes due to instinct or maturation (crawling, standing, walking), illness or drugs are not learning. Learning is not directly observed; it is inferred from improved performance (errors decrease with practice). Learning helps us adapt to the environment and is lifelong.

Discovered by the Russian scientist Ivan P. Pavlov, who worked with dogs. Food is the unconditioned stimulus (UCS) and salivation to food the unconditioned response (UCR). A tone or buzzer (neutral stimulus) is paired repeatedly with food; after pairing the buzzer alone, now the conditioned stimulus (CS), produces salivation, the conditioned response (CR). Acquisition is the phase of repeated pairing. If the CS is presented without the UCS, the CR gradually disappears: extinction. After a rest gap the CR may reappear for a few trials on presenting the CS: spontaneous recovery.

Organisms learn to repeat behaviours that produce positive outcomes and avoid or escape negative ones. B.F. Skinner studied it in rats using the Skinner Box with a lever: a hungry rat presses the lever accidentally, gets a food pellet, and gradually learns to press it; the behaviour is instrumental in getting food, and is an operation on the environment. Reinforcement is any operation that increases the rate of response. Positive reinforcement is a reward (food) that strengthens the response. Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus (e.g. electric shock) when the response occurs; it includes escape learning (the rat escapes the shock) and avoidance learning (the rat avoids the shock). 'Negative' refers to the aversive nature of the reinforcer, and it is still reinforcement as it increases the response.

In continuous reinforcement every correct response is reinforced; it is useful for establishing new behaviours. In partial (intermittent) reinforcement only some responses are reinforced; it is more powerful for maintaining acquired behaviour.

Learning new skills by observing the behaviour of others (models), e.g. children learn aggression from violence on TV and learn social roles. It is more complex than imitation, since information may be learnt but not put to immediate use. Appropriate role models influence youngsters positively.
## Other types: verbal, concept and skill learning

Verbal learning is the learning of language (serial learning, paired-associate learning). Concept learning is developing categories of objects and events (boys, fruits; abstract concepts: love, freedom, democracy; concrete: cow, table); one response is made to all stimuli of a category and concepts reduce the complexity of the world. Skill learning is acquiring skills such as riding a bicycle, car driving, piloting; with over-learning a skill becomes automatic and one can do two tasks at once.

Using earlier learning in a new situation. Positive transfer: the first learning helps the second (multiplication used in the market). Negative transfer: the first learning interferes with the second. Zero transfer: neither helps nor interferes.

Study at a specific quiet place; use spaced sessions (spaced practice) rather than massed practice; use memory aids; test yourself; over-learn (study beyond bare mastery); avoid procrastination using a time schedule and specific goals.

vsa: Learning is a relatively durable change in behaviour due to experience, e.g. a child making fewer errors in writing the alphabet with practice.
Why are crawling and walking not examples of learning?
They are changes due to maturation, not experience or practice.
Increasing the rate of a response by removing an aversive stimulus (e.g. electric shock) when the response occurs.
Differentiate between continuous and partial reinforcement.
In continuous reinforcement every correct response is reinforced; in partial reinforcement only some responses are reinforced.
What is observational learning? Give an example.
Learning by observing the behaviour of models, e.g. children learning aggression from violence on TV.
Developing categories of objects and events so that one response is made to all stimuli in a category, e.g. 'fruit'.
What is skill learning? Give two examples.
Acquiring skills that become automatic with practice, e.g. riding a bicycle and driving a car.
sa: Describe Pavlov's experiment on classical conditioning.

A hungry dog was given food (UCS) producing salivation (UCR). A buzzer (CS) was paired repeatedly with food. After several pairings the buzzer alone produced salivation (CR), showing that learning by association had occurred.

If the buzzer is presented again and again without food, salivation gradually stops (extinction). After a rest gap, presenting the buzzer alone again brings back salivation for a few trials (spontaneous recovery).
Describe Skinner's experiment on operant conditioning.

A hungry rat in the Skinner Box moves randomly and accidentally presses a lever, receiving a food pellet. With repeated trials, activity centres around the lever and the rat learns that pressing it gives food; the response is reinforced and learned.
Distinguish positive and negative reinforcement with examples.

Positive reinforcement is a reward such as food that strengthens the response preceding it. Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus such as shock when the response occurs, which also increases the response (escape and avoidance learning).
Explain transfer of training and its types.
Transfer is using earlier learning in a new situation. It is positive when the first learning helps the second, negative when it interferes, and zero when it neither helps nor interferes.
Give any three tips for better study habits.
Study at a fixed quiet place; use spaced sessions rather than one long massed session; self-test and over-learn; avoid procrastination.
la: Explain the process of classical conditioning with the help of Pavlov's experiment.

Pavlov, a Russian scientist, studied dogs. Food (UCS) produces salivation (UCR). A buzzer (CS) causes only an orienting response before conditioning. During acquisition, buzzer and food are paired repeatedly; the dog then salivates (CR) to the buzzer alone. If the buzzer is given without food, extinction occurs; after a rest, spontaneous recovery of CR appears for a few trials.
Explain operant conditioning and the role of reinforcement.

Operant conditioning is a process in which organisms repeat behaviours that give positive outcomes or avoid negative ones. Skinner's rat in the Skinner Box learned to press a lever for food. Reinforcement increases the rate of response: positive reinforcement (reward), negative reinforcement (removal of aversive stimulus, escape and avoidance learning). Continuous reinforcement establishes behaviour and partial reinforcement maintains it.
Describe observational learning, concept learning, skill learning and verbal learning.

Observational learning is learning by watching models (aggression from TV, social roles). Concept learning forms categories (concrete and abstract). Skill learning is acquiring skills like cycling, driving that become automatic. Verbal learning is learning language through serial and paired-associate learning.
What is learning? Discuss transfer of training and ways to improve study habits.

Learning is a relatively durable change in behaviour due to experience. Transfer is the use of earlier learning in new situations (positive, negative, zero). For better learning: study at a specific place, use spaced sessions, memory aids, self-testing, over-learning and avoid procrastination.
